The deadly triad

Three ingredients that every large-scale value method wants: function approximation, bootstrapping, and off-policy learning. Any two together are safe. All three together can make the weights grow without limit, even when the true values are all zero.

Two states, one weight

S&B §11.2. Both estimates share one weight $w$: the first state's is $w$, the second's is $2w$. The first leads to the second with reward 0. Only that transition gets updated, as can happen off-policy.

$\hat v = w$1
reward 0
→
$\hat v = 2w$2
reward 0
→ end

Baird's counterexample

S&B Example 11.1. Seven states, eight weights, every reward 0, $\gamma = 0.99$, so every true value is 0 and $\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{0}$ represents them exactly. The behaviour policy $b$ takes the dashed action (to one of the six top states) with probability $6/7$ and the solid action (to the bottom state) with probability $1/7$. The target policy $\pi$ always takes the solid action.

The maths

Two states. Semi-gradient TD(0) at the first state, where $\nabla \hat v = 1$:

$$w_{t+1} = w_t + \alpha\,\big[0 + \gamma \cdot 2w_t - w_t\big] \cdot 1 = \big(1 + \alpha(2\gamma - 1)\big)\, w_t .$$

The factor is above 1 whenever $\gamma > 0.5$, so $w$ grows geometrically for any $\alpha > 0$. Raising $w$ to shrink the error at the first state raises the target $2\gamma w$ even more. If the second state is updated too (target 0, $\nabla \hat v = 2$), it multiplies $w$ by $1 - 4\alpha$, which pulls it back. On-policy, the second state is always visited after the first, so that correction always happens.

Baird. Off-policy semi-gradient TD(0) weights each update by the importance-sampling ratio $\rho_t = \pi(A_t \mid S_t)/b(A_t \mid S_t)$ (Lesson 39):

$$\mathbf{w}_{t+1} = \mathbf{w}_t + \alpha\,\rho_t\,\delta_t\,\mathbf{x}(S_t), \qquad \delta_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma\,\hat v(S_{t+1}, \mathbf{w}_t) - \hat v(S_t, \mathbf{w}_t).$$

Here $\rho_t = 1/(1/7) = 7$ for the solid action and $0$ for the dashed one. With $\alpha = 0.01$ and $\mathbf{w} = (1,1,1,1,1,1,10,1)$ the weights diverge, and S&B note the expected update diverges for any positive step size.

Why. In expectation, linear semi-gradient TD is $\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} + \alpha(\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{A}\mathbf{w})$ with

$$\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{D}\,(\mathbf{I} - \gamma \mathbf{P}_\pi)\,\mathbf{X},$$

where the rows of $\mathbf{X}$ are the feature vectors, $\mathbf{D}$ is diagonal with the distribution of states being updated, and $\mathbf{P}_\pi$ holds the target policy's transition probabilities. The iteration is stable when $\mathbf{A}$ is positive definite. If $\mathbf{D}$ is the on-policy distribution of $\pi$, it is (S&B §9.4). Off-policy, $\mathbf{D}$ comes from $b$ and the guarantee is gone.

Remove any one leg and the problem goes away. Tabular features make every state its own weight, so no update can drag another state's value. Monte Carlo targets do not depend on $\mathbf{w}$, so the update is true gradient descent. On-policy updates restore the positive-definite $\mathbf{A}$. In Baird's example the "on-policy" setting evaluates $b$ itself ($\rho = 1$), and "no bootstrapping" uses the return, which is 0 here for every trajectory.

S&B §11.3 calls this combination the deadly triad. DQN (Lessons 66 to 69) has all three, and much of its design is about surviving them.
